The plugin registers an instance of the link:{springapi}/org/springframework/cache/CacheManager.html[CacheManager] interface as the `grailsCacheManager` Spring bean, so it's easy to access using dependency injection.

The most common method you would call on the `grailsCacheManager` is `getCache(String name)` to access a link:{springapi}/org/springframework/cache/Cache.html[Cache] instance programmatically. This shouldn't be needed often however. From the `Cache` instance you can also access the underlying cache implementation using `cache.getNativeCache()`.

The cache tags cache with the `grailsCacheManager` bean, which they are given by name. A cache provider plugin replaces it by defining a bean of that name, and an application can do the same with a `GrailsCacheManager` of its own.

The cache annotations, and `GrailsCacheAdminService`, are given their cache manager by type, as Spring injects one. Where the application context has another cache manager too, such as one the application defines for Spring's own caching, or the one the Spring Security plugin defines when `cacheUsers` is set, Spring chooses between them as it does for any injection: the one marked primary, for example, or the one with the highest `@Priority`. Only where Spring cannot choose, because none of them is marked primary or has a `@Priority` above the others, and `grailsCacheManager` is one of the cache managers it could inject, do the annotations use `grailsCacheManager`. Two cache managers both marked primary, or sharing the highest `@Priority`, still fail to start, as Spring rejects them before it looks further. A cache manager whose `@Priority` is only on the object its factory method or `FactoryBean` returns, with the declared type a plain `CacheManager`, is not seen as preferred beside `grailsCacheManager`, which the annotations then use; mark it primary to keep it. So with a cache manager of the application's own marked primary, the annotations cache with that one, while the cache tags still cache with `grailsCacheManager`.

A cache manager may have no cache of the name an annotation gives, as a `JCacheCacheManager` has none it was not configured with. The annotated method then runs uncached, and a warning names the class and the cache once for each cache manager.
